story.card_text: Donald McKay built his clippers in East Boston, but the monument paid for by private subscription in 1933 went here, to Castle Island in South Boston. Read the northeast face. It opens with the Flying Cloud, then McKay, 1810-1880, 'master-builder whose genius produced ships of beauty and speed before unknown.' Under that, the Great Republic, launched October 4, 1853: 4,555 tons register, 325 feet long, 'the largest ship in the world when launched.' Then the lists. Count the names under Clippers: thirty-one, the same as the Harborwalk sign in Eastie. The Landmarks Commission says thirty. Two against one, and the granite was here first. Now look northeast. The end of runway 4R is about 1.3 kilometers away, and by FAA coordinates this spot sits about 570 meters beside the line planes fly in on. In 2015 4R took 29 percent of jet arrivals, more than any other runway. When the wind is northeast, they come past you low.
story.headline: McKay's monument stands in Southie, off the end of the runway that took the most Logan jet arrivals in 2015.
story.look_now: Read the ship lists, then turn northeast and watch for an arrival lining up for 4R.
story.narration_script: This is the Donald McKay monument. He built his ships across the water in East Boston, but this is where his admirers put his monument, in nineteen thirty-three. The first words on this face are a ship's name, the Flying Cloud. Then McKay, and the Great Republic, launched in eighteen fifty-three and called the largest ship in the world. Then the lists of ships. Count the clippers: thirty-one, the same number as the sign in East Boston. The city's landmarks commission says thirty. Now look northeast toward the airport. The end of runway four right is a little over a kilometer away, and you're standing just beside the path planes take to land on it. In twenty fifteen, more jets landed on four right than on any other runway at Logan. When the wind is from the northeast, they come right past you.

pitch_60: In nineteen sixty-seven, the T dropped a word from a station name in East Boston. The word was park. The park was forty-six acres of Olmsted on the harbor, and the airport had just made it runway. Flight Path is a riddle walk through Eastie and the airport that kept growing next to it. Logan started in nineteen twenty-three as two cinder strips, smoothed by a pair of draft horses. You'll find the sign that says what the ferry cost, the clipper the captain's wife navigated around Cape Horn, and the lightship that exists because Titanic's sister ran down the one before it. You'll stand on the street where mothers with baby carriages stopped the dump trucks, and on the road where the elms came down in one morning. Every answer is something you read off the street. It ends in a salt marsh about a mile off the end of a runway, where, in a southwest wind, the jets come in low over the reeds. It starts at Maverick, on the Blue Line. Check the wind.

seo.landing_copy:
Logan Airport didn't land in East Boston. It was filled in, a few hundred acres at a time, starting in 1923 with two cinder strips at Jeffries Point. This walk follows that history from the ground, using the Blue Line to hop between clusters, and it ends at one of the best places in Boston to watch jets come in low.

You'll start where the harbor ferries ran and where the streetcar tunnel under the harbor came up into Maverick Square. You'll meet the clipper ship that ran from New York to San Francisco in eighty-nine days and the woman who navigated it. You'll find the lightship built because Titanic's sister sank the one before it, and walk the waterfront parks Massport built. The walk is honest about why it built them.

Then it turns inland. One stop up the Blue Line is a station that dropped a word from its name in 1967 because the park it was named for, Frederick Law Olmsted's Wood Island Park, was being bulldozed for a runway. Down the street is a small park that marks where the houses of Neptune Road stood. A few blocks away, in 1968, a group of mothers with baby carriages stopped the airport's dump trucks, and they won.

The last two stops are for the plane people. We tell you which runways you're looking at, which wind direction brings arrivals over your head, and why, using FAA and Massport records and not guesswork. Bring a long lens. If you run an ADS-B receiver, you'll want it on.

Every fact is sourced: Boston Landmarks Commission reports, Boston Public Library archival photos, FAA records of decision, Massport runway-use counts, contemporary reporting. Where sources disagree, we tell you both versions. Thirteen stops, about two and three-quarter hours, or a one-hour Blue Line cut. Any two stops are free, and the pack is $1.99.

story.card_text: On July 22, 1927, two months after Paris, Charles Lindbergh brought the Spirit of St. Louis into the East Boston airfield, and this bronze puts his plane on the same wall as a Revolutionary skirmish. Theodore Barbarossa cast the relief in 1975 for the elderly housing behind you; a city trust fund paid to restore it in 2012. Read it left to right. May 27, 1775: Colonel Stark's volunteers drive livestock off Noddle's and Hog Islands so the British can't eat them, and the skirmish ends with HMS Diana burned. Then the Flying Cloud, built a few blocks north, and the woman who navigated it. Then the immigrants: Canadian, Irish, Russian and Eastern European Jewish, Italian. Then the plane. The last panel is the one that sets up this walk: tunnels, a highway and the airport changed the neighborhood. That's the polite version. The next twelve stops are the rest of it.

story.narration_script: Find the bronze relief on Lewis Mall, the one with five scenes. Everything around you used to be an island called Noddle's Island. In May of seventeen seventy-five, colonial volunteers drove the cattle off it so the British couldn't eat them, and the fight ended with a British warship on fire. The next panel is a clipper ship, built a few blocks from here. Then the people who came: Canadian, Irish, Jewish, Italian. Then a plane. On July twenty-second, nineteen twenty-seven, Charles Lindbergh landed the Spirit of Saint Louis at the East Boston airfield, two months after Paris. The last panel says tunnels, a highway and an airport changed the neighborhood. That's the polite version. The rest of this walk is the long one.

story.card_text: A ride from here to the city cost one cent a person, and on the Fourth of July it was free. One resident's grandfather collected the fares; a horse and team paid five cents. Ferries ran from East Boston from 1834, at one point on three separate routes, and they carried pushcarts and the occasional Model T. Then the city dug under the water. Crews tunneling from both sides met beneath the harbor on July 4, 1903, and the streetcar tunnel opened at the end of 1904 - the Harborwalk sign calls it the first underwater subway in the U.S., and it's today's Blue Line. Not everyone trusted it: one teacher's mother kept taking the ferry, sitting in the companionway so her hat wouldn't blow off. The Sumner Tunnel opened for cars in 1934, and the sign calls that the beginning of the end for the ferries. The last East Boston ferry crossed in 1952. Mario Carco, who sold newspapers on the Lewis Street ferry, remembered the pilot throwing the props into reverse and the boat slamming into the timbers and sliding into the dock.
story.headline: A ferry ride from here to the city cost one cent, and it was free on the Fourth of July.
story.look_now: Look straight across the water at the North End and downtown. That's the trip the penny paid for.
story.narration_script: Find the sign called Crossing the Harbor. From eighteen thirty-four, ferries ran from here to Boston. One resident's grandfather collected the fares: one cent a person, five cents for a horse and wagon, and free on the Fourth of July. Then Boston went under the water. Two tunnel crews digging from opposite sides met under the harbor on the Fourth of July, nineteen oh three. The streetcar tunnel opened the next year. You rode it here: it's the Blue Line. Some people didn't trust it. One woman kept taking the ferry anyway and sat in the passageway so her hat wouldn't blow off. Then the Sumner Tunnel opened for cars in nineteen thirty-four. That was the beginning of the end for the ferries. The last East Boston ferry crossed in nineteen fifty-two.

story.card_text: This park exists because the Port Authority took a bigger one. When it destroyed Frederick Law Olmsted's Wood Island Park for Logan, the architecture guide to Massachusetts says, it reclaimed this derelict waterfront parcel for new open space. Piers Park opened in the mid-1990s on 6.5 acres: a brick promenade, shade pavilions, and the skyline straight across the water. The pavilion at the tip is dedicated to Donald McKay, Master Shipbuilder. Next door, Piers Park II opened in December 2023, and Massport says it now runs about thirty-eight acres of green space in East Boston. Wood Island Park alone was forty-six. Just east of here, in what is now the shipyard, the federal government ran Boston's immigration station from 1920 to about 1954; by the Landmarks Commission's estimate, perhaps one arrival in ten was held there for an exam, a hearing or detention. In the Second World War it held German, Italian and Japanese residents classed as enemy aliens. It was being torn down by January 2011, and nothing marks the spot.

story.card_text: On May 15, 1934, in fog, the liner Olympic, Titanic's sister, ran down the Nantucket lightship LV-117 on its station off the Nantucket Shoals. Seven of the eleven men aboard died. This ship is the replacement: LV-112, built in 1936 by Pusey and Jones in Wilmington, Delaware, and by the National Park Service's account the largest lightship ever built in the United States. The usual version is that the British government paid for it. The National Register nomination says the White Star Line paid the United States government $500,000 in reparations; the ship cost about $301,000, per the museum that owns it. Her station sat on the shipping lane from Europe, 47 miles from the nearest land by the Park Service's count; the museum puts it at 100 miles from the mainland and calls it the farthest offshore. In the Second World War she was painted gray and worked as an examination vessel off Portland, Maine. She retired in 1975 and is a National Historic Landmark. The United States Lightship Museum towed her to Boston in May 2010, and on August 7, 2015, her beacon was lit for the first time in about forty years.

story.narration_script: Look for the red ship. On May fifteenth, nineteen thirty-four, in fog, the ocean liner Olympic, the Titanic's sister ship, ran straight into the lightship that marked the Nantucket Shoals. Seven of the eleven men on board died. This ship is the replacement, built in nineteen thirty-six. The National Park Service calls it the largest lightship ever built in this country. You'll hear that the British government paid for it. The official record says the White Star Line, which owned the Olympic, paid the United States government five hundred thousand dollars. Its job was to sit still, about fifty miles past Nantucket, and shine. During the Second World War it was painted gray and stood guard off Portland, Maine. It retired in nineteen seventy-five, came to Boston in twenty ten, and in the summer of twenty fifteen they lit the beacon again for the first time in about forty years.

story.card_text: In 1922 the state legislature put up $250,000 for an airfield, on the condition that someone match it, and the Boston Chamber of Commerce did. Officers of the Massachusetts National Guard's 101st squadron had lobbied for the field, and they picked Jeffries Point because the flats next to it belonged to the state and could be filled. What opened in 1923 was 189 acres with two cinder runways about 1,500 feet long, laid out in a T. The Massachusetts Aviation Historical Society says a pair of draft horses dragged a wooden sledge over the cinders to smooth them. A note on the back of an Army Air Service photo in the Boston Public Library records the first landing: June 13, 1923, Lieutenant Kitchell Snow. The official dedication came on September 8, with Mayor Curley starting an air race out to Boston Light. The next day's Globe: 'Boston's Air Port at Jeffries Point, east Boston was officially opened yesterday - and opened good!' It was renamed for General Edward Lawrence Logan of South Boston in 1943. Almost everything you see across the water was mud flats then.

What opened in nineteen twenty-three was one hundred eighty-nine acres and two cinder runways, each about fifteen hundred feet long. A pair of draft horses dragged a wooden sledge over the cinders to smooth them out. The first landing was June thirteenth, nineteen twenty-three. story.card_text: In 1968 Massport was filling the Bird Island Flats to grow the airport, and the fill came by dump truck straight down Maverick Street, a narrow residential street full of kids and old people. The trucks were fast and heavy, and residents said they were cracking houses. Meetings with Massport went nowhere. So after a meeting with State Representative George DiLorenzo, the women of the street decided to block the trucks, and on September 28, 1968, they did. Only women and children took part, on purpose, to keep it from turning into a fight. Most pushed baby carriages. The Eastie Times names Anna DeFronzo and Karen Maddalena as leaders. State Police dragged and pushed them to the sidewalk. Then Mayor Kevin White sent the Boston Police, who stopped the trucks instead. Massport agreed to move its trucks onto routes on its own property. An eleven-minute film of the protest survives; Giordana Mecagni, Northeastern's university archivist and an Eastie resident, restored it; the Eastie Times reported it in 2021. In 2015 Massport put a replica of a 1970s city panel honoring the mothers on the path behind these houses.
story.headline: Mothers with baby carriages stopped Massport's trucks on Maverick Street, and won.
story.look_now: Look down Maverick Street toward the airport and picture loaded dump trucks coming at you. In daylight, find the mothers' panel on the path behind the houses.
story.narration_script: You're on Maverick Street. In nineteen sixty-eight, Massport was filling in the mud flats to make the airport bigger, and the dirt came by dump truck, straight down this street. It's narrow, and it was full of kids and old people. Meetings with Massport got nowhere. So on September twenty-eighth, nineteen sixty-eight, the women of this street blocked the trucks. Only women and children, on purpose, so it wouldn't turn into a fight. Most of them were pushing baby carriages. Anna DeFronzo and Karen Maddalena were among the leaders. The State Police dragged and pushed them to the sidewalk. Then the mayor sent the Boston Police, and the Boston Police stopped the trucks. Massport moved its trucks onto its own land. The mothers won. In twenty fifteen, Massport put up a copy of an old city sign in their honor, on the path behind these houses.

story.card_text: This park was offered partly as an apology, in partial restitution for Wood Island Park, which Massport had destroyed about twenty years before the state took this land. It still took until 2007 to open. The strip was a railroad first: the Grand Junction's tracks ran to the East Boston docks, and Conrail abandoned this section in the 1970s. The old yards north of Route 1A turned into a private Park'N'Fly lot for Logan. Then the Big Dig needed a third harbor tunnel, which would send more traffic to the airport, and in 1989 the state highway department started eminent domain proceedings here. It took a scandal over the land taking and a swap before Massport bought the land outright in 2001. The park opened in 2007: 18 acres, playing fields, paths, and a community garden that started that July with forty-six plots. The Leventhal Map Center calls Bremen Street Park and East Boston Memorial Park buffers between the neighborhood and the airport. That's what they are. When the wind is from the northwest, departures off runway 33L climb out over Eagle Hill, behind you. Since 2007, a Massport advisory committee member counted, 33L has handled about one Logan departure in six.
story.headline: Bremen Street Park was built partly to make up for Wood Island Park - forty years late.
story.look_now: Look east past the fields toward the airport fence, then up - northwest-wind departures off runway 33L climb over this side of East Boston.
story.narration_script: You're in Bremen Street Park. This was railroad land, then a parking lot for airport travelers. When the Big Dig added a third tunnel under the harbor, the state took this land and promised a park. Part of the reason, in the words of the time, was restitution for Wood Island Park, which Massport had destroyed about twenty years earlier. After a long fight over the land deal, Massport bought it in two thousand one. The park opened in two thousand seven. Eighteen acres, ball fields, and a community garden with forty-six plots. It's a nice park. It's also a buffer between the houses and the airport. Look up. If planes are taking off to the northwest today, they're climbing right over Eagle Hill. Since two thousand seven, that's been about one Logan departure in six.

story.card_text: This station's name is missing a word, and the word was a park. It opened on January 5, 1952, when the Blue Line pushed out past Airport, as Day Square. On October 21, 1954 it became Wood Island Park, for the park next door. Early in 1967 the MBTA dropped the last word, because Massport was destroying the park for the airport. It was Frederick Law Olmsted's design: about forty-six acres on the harbor, opened in 1898, with beaches, a bathhouse, tennis courts, ball fields, a running track and an outdoor gymnasium. A preliminary plan from about 1884 survives at the Leventhal Map Center. People who grew up here compare it to the Common. Massport took it in the 1960s and used the land to extend runway 15R/33L, now the airport's longest at 10,083 feet. The station sign is one of the few places the name survives. Before the subway, the narrow-gauge Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn ran a Wood Island stop a few blocks away at Prescott Street from 1875 until the railroad shut down in 1940.

story.card_text: Neptune Road was the way into Wood Island Park: in the Trust for Public Land's words, a parkway of stately elms Olmsted designed as the approach to the park entrance. Fred Salvucci, who ran the city's Little City Hall in East Boston, called it the most prestigious street in East Boston. Families lived on both sides. Massport, then run by Edward J. King, took the park in 1967. Then it came for the road. Early on the morning of April 23, 1969, without notice, Massport crews arrived with bulldozers and chainsaws, backed by state police, and began dropping the elms before residents could get into the street. story.card_text: Constitution Beach was built between December 1949 and May 1951 from about thirty-four acres of hydraulically dredged fill and gravel, and opened in 1952. In Eastie it's Shays Beach. The state rebuilt the bathhouse in the late 1990s, and the blue footbridge over the tracks was named for Anthony and Dee Dee Marmo in 2001. Across the water are runways 22L and 22R. Wikipedia says about 2,000 feet; measured from FAA coordinates, the end of 22R, where departures start their roll, is about 2,700 feet from the middle of the beach, and 22L is about three-quarters of a mile. When the wind is from the southwest, the FAA tower's southwest setup lands planes on 22L and 27 and departs them on 22L and 22R. How often? In 2015, Massport's count put 31 percent of jet departures on 22R, more than any other runway. Planes taxiing to 22R wait at a noise hold line on the taxiway called November, and a state rule says nobody lands on 22R or takes off from 4L between 11 at night and 6 in the morning. Spotters say: afternoons, a long lens. Your view here is from the side, so you'll see the planes roll and lift off. For planes coming in low overhead, go to the last stop.

In Eastie it's Shays Beach. Look across the water. Those are runways twenty-two left and twenty-two right. The near end of twenty-two right is about half a mile away. On a southwest wind, the control tower lands planes on twenty-two left and twenty-seven, and sends them off on twenty-two left and twenty-two right. You'll see departures line up on the taxiway and roll toward the city. In twenty fifteen, almost a third of the jets leaving Logan took off on twenty-two right. Overnight, from eleven at night to six in the morning, nobody's allowed to land on twenty-two right. From here you watch from the side. For planes coming in low over your head, go to the next stop.

story.card_text: Eastie built the ships and Southie got the monument. Donald McKay built this house in 1844 and lived here until 1877, two blocks up from his yard on Border Street between White and Eutaw Streets. Enoch Train backed the yard. McKay's first clipper was the Staghound in 1850. The Flying Cloud came the next year. The Great Republic, launched October 4, 1853, was called the largest ship in the world: 4,555 tons register and 325 feet long. The granite obelisk to McKay, put up by private subscription in 1933, is at Castle Island in South Boston, across the harbor. Eastie has a smaller granite stone at 400 Border Street, the Globe says, carved 'famous clippers built on this site by Donald McKay.' The Landmarks Commission studied this house and recommended it for landmark designation. It's still a private home. In June 2022 a side wall of the old carriage house on the property, facing Brooks Street, gave way under a rotting roof.
story.headline: Eastie built Donald McKay's ships. Southie got his monument.

story.narration_script: This is Donald McKay's house. He built it in eighteen forty-four and lived here until eighteen seventy-seven, two blocks uphill from his shipyard on Border Street. The Flying Cloud came out of that yard in eighteen fifty-one. The Great Republic came out in eighteen fifty-three and was called the biggest ship in the world: three hundred twenty-five feet long. If you came looking for the big McKay monument, it isn't here. The granite obelisk, put up in nineteen thirty-three, is at Castle Island in South Boston. East Boston got a smaller stone down on Border Street. The city's landmarks commission recommended protecting this house. It's still somebody's home, so stay on the sidewalk. In June of twenty twenty-two, part of the old carriage house out back fell in under a rotting roof.
